problem: VLMs such as GPT-4V and Gemini only output text. They struggle to produce precise continuous spatial outputs such as navigation waypoints, end-effector motions or image coordinates. Prior visual prompting (e.g. Set-of-Mark) relies on fixed proposals or a separate perception system to create the marks.
motivation: Many embodied problems are inherently spatial: choosing a waypoint for a mobile robot, moving an arm, localizing a keypoint. Solving them zero-shot with off-the-shelf VLMs, with no robot data, would give highly general controllers. The driving observation is that VLMs are bad at emitting precise coordinates but good at picking among a few labelled visual choices, and repeated coarse choices can be refined into precise ones.
key_idea: Cast continuous spatial and action inference as iterative multiple-choice VQA. Draw sampled candidate actions as numbered arrows or markers on the image, let the VLM pick the best ones, fit a new sampling distribution to the picks, and repeat, in the style of the cross-entropy method.
insight: Lifting actions into the VLM's native image+text space works better than asking for textual actions. On offline navigation, arrow annotations beat a 3x3-grid text baseline: L2 0.21 vs 0.26 in-view, 0.23 vs 0.35 semantic, with much lower variance. Robustness comes mostly from parallel calls. On the real robot, 'No Iteration / 3 Parallel' is as good as or better than '3 Iterations / 3 Parallel' on most navigation tasks, and extra iterations or parallel calls give diminishing returns offline. More samples gives better initial coverage but worse optimization because crowded markers occlude each other; about 10 samples was the best trade-off. Out-of-view navigation targets stay hard (L2 about 0.37-0.44 regardless of settings), exposing the limits of single-image reactive selection. Performance rises monotonically with Gemini model size.
method: Visual prompt mapping Ω: projects candidate actions into the image as arrows from the robot/end-effector (or from the image bottom-centre for navigation), labelled with circled numbers. For 3D actions, depth is encoded by arrow colour (red→blue) and circle size.

Iterative optimization (CEM-like): sample M candidates (about 10) from an isotropic Gaussian P_A^(i), annotate the image, ask the VLM (chain-of-thought, multiple-choice) for the top-K labels, refit the Gaussian to the selected actions, and repeat for N iterations (typically 3).
Parallel calls: run E independent PIVOT instances (e.g. 3). Aggregate by fitting a distribution to the E outputs or by re-querying the VLM to pick the single best.
Navigation grounding: the selected pixel direction is lifted to a 3D target using the on-board depth camera, and the robot moves toward it (max 1.0 m per step), closed-loop.
Manipulation grounding: arrows encode relative Cartesian (x,y,z) end-effector deltas; gripper open/close is expressed in text; rotations are fixed.
Prompt design: zero-shot CoT with prompt order preamble → image → task. Few-shot direct prompting is nearly as good and more token-efficient.

setting.backbone: GPT-4V (frozen) by default; four sizes of Gemini (frozen) for scaling study

setting.action_space: navigation: 2D image-space direction/target lifted to 3D target via depth (≤1.0 m per step); manipulation: 4D relative Cartesian (x,y,z) + gripper; RAVENS: pick-and-place pixels
setting.simulator: real world (mobile manipulator, Franka) + RAVENS simulator for tabletop pick-and-place

numbers_note: RefCOCO (1000 random testA examples), RAVENS, the offline manipulation ablations (cosine similarity), the prompt ablations and the Gemini scaling results are reported only in figures, so no numbers were extracted for them. The real-world navigation table gives per-task success only, with no average and no explicit trial count (the 25% increments suggest 4 trials). No standard embodied-navigation benchmark is evaluated.
results: PIVOT gives non-zero zero-shot success on real-robot navigation and manipulation with a frozen GPT-4V and no robot data. Real-world navigation success reaches 75-100% per task with parallel calls, up from 25% on three of four tasks for a single call. On offline navigation, image-annotation prompting beats a text-only 3x3-grid baseline (e.g. semantic L2 0.23 vs 0.35), and iterations plus parallel calls lower L2 further (in-view 0.21→0.17). No trained or external methods are compared; the only baselines are text-only prompting and ablated PIVOT variants.
limitations: Current VLMs cannot reliably reason about depth encoded in annotations (3D and rotation actions are poorly handled). Fine-grained, contact-rich control degrades under occlusion near objects.
The VLM behaves greedily and myopically on multi-step tasks, and sometimes attaches correct reasoning to the wrong arrow label. Out-of-view navigation targets remain hard.
Evaluation is small-scale and custom (4 navigation tasks, a 60-example offline set, a few trials each), with no standard benchmark and no comparison to trained methods.
